prompt: Rewrite this sentence so that it is about two dogs: 'The dog barks at the postman every morning.'

key_points.text: Uses a plural subject (the dogs, two dogs)
Uses the plural verb bark, with no -s

model_answers: The two dogs bark at the postman every morning.
The dogs bark at the postman every morning.

guards.note: 'dogs barks' keeps the singular verb
the subject must be plural

anchors.text: The two dogs bark at the postman every morning.
The two dogs barks at the postman every morning.
The dog bark at the postman every morning.

rationale: Produces agreement with a plural subject; the -s must be removed, not just recognised as wrong.

prompt: Finish the sentence with the right form of be and your own ending: 'The box of old toys ...'

key_points.text: Uses is or was, agreeing with 'box', not with 'toys'
Completes the sentence sensibly

model_answers: The box of old toys is in the cupboard.
The box of old toys was too heavy to lift.

guards.note: the verb must agree with 'box'

anchors.text: The box of old toys is under my bed.
The box of old toys are under my bed.
The box of old toys was given to my cousin.

rationale: Agreement across an intervening plural noun, produced in the learner's own sentence.

prompt: Rewrite in the past, starting with 'Yesterday': 'Every day I go to the market and buy some fruit.'

key_points.text: Uses went
Uses bought

model_answers: Yesterday I went to the market and bought some fruit.

guards.note: went is the past of go
bought is the past of buy

anchors.text: Yesterday I went to the market and bought some fruit.
Yesterday I went to the market and buyed some fruit.
Yesterday I go to the market and buy some fruit.

rationale: Two common irregular past forms produced in one sentence.

prompt: This story is in the past, but two verbs slip into the present. Rewrite it correctly: 'We reached the beach at noon. The sea looks calm, so we decide to swim.'

key_points.text: Changes looks to looked
Changes decide to decided

model_answers: We reached the beach at noon. The sea looked calm, so we decided to swim.

guards.note: looked is needed
decided is needed

anchors.text: We reached the beach at noon. The sea looked calm, so we decided to swim.
We reached the beach at noon. The sea looked calm, so we decide to swim.
We reach the beach at noon. The sea looks calm, so we decide to swim.

rationale: Keeps tense consistent across two sentences; both slips must be found.

prompt: Finish the sentence: 'If it rains tomorrow, ...'

key_points.text: Uses will (or won't, or going to) and a verb in the result
The result makes sense

model_answers: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If it rains tomorrow, the match won't happen.

guards.note: a first conditional uses will, not would

anchors.text: If it rains tomorrow, we will play indoors.
If it rains tomorrow, we would play indoors.
If it rains tomorrow, I will take my umbrella.

rationale: Produces the result clause of a first conditional.

prompt: Finish the sentence about an imaginary situation: 'If I could fly, ...'

key_points.text: Uses would, could or might and a verb in the result
The result makes sense

model_answers: If I could fly, I would visit my grandmother every weekend.

guards.note: an imaginary result needs would, could or might

anchors.text: If I could fly, I would visit my grandmother every weekend.
If I could fly, I will go to the moon.
If I could fly, I'd go to school over the traffic.

rationale: Produces the result clause of a second conditional.

prompt: Join these into one sentence starting with 'If': 'I didn't hear the alarm. I was late for school.'

key_points.text: Uses had heard in the if-clause
Uses would not have been (or wouldn't have been) late in the result

model_answers: If I had heard the alarm, I wouldn't have been late for school.
If I had heard the alarm, I would not have been late for school.

guards.note: the if-clause needs had heard
the result needs would have been

anchors.text: If I had heard the alarm, I wouldn't have been late for school.
If I heard the alarm, I wouldn't be late for school.
If I had heard the alarm, I won't have been late.

rationale: Builds a third conditional from two facts, reversing both.

prompt: Report what Ravi said: 'I am tired.' Start with 'Ravi said that'.

key_points.text: Changes I to he
Changes am to was

model_answers: Ravi said that he was tired.

guards.note: the pronoun must change to he
am must change to was

anchors.text: Ravi said that he was tired.
Ravi said that he is tired.
Ravi said that I was tired.

rationale: Pronoun and tense changes produced, not chosen.

prompt: Report the question. Mira asked me: 'Where do you live?'

key_points.text: Uses statement word order (where I lived), with no do or did
Changes you to I and live to lived

model_answers: Mira asked me where I lived.

guards.note: a reported question keeps statement order
needs I and lived

anchors.text: Mira asked me where I lived.
Mira asked me where did I live.
Mira asked me where I live.

rationale: A reported wh-question: word order, pronoun and tense together.

prompt: Join into one sentence using who or which: 'I have a cousin. She plays the sitar.'

key_points.text: Uses who (or that) for the person
Does not repeat she

model_answers: I have a cousin who plays the sitar.

guards.note: which is not used for a person
she must not be repeated

anchors.text: I have a cousin who plays the sitar.
I have a cousin which plays the sitar.
I have a cousin who she plays the sitar.

rationale: Joins with a relative pronoun for a person, without a resumptive pronoun.

prompt: Join into one sentence using whose: 'That is the girl. Her painting won the prize.'

key_points.text: Uses whose before painting
Leaves out her

model_answers: That is the girl whose painting won the prize.

guards.note: whose must come before painting
her must be left out

anchors.text: That is the girl whose painting won the prize.
That is the girl who her painting won the prize.
That's the girl whose painting won the prize.

rationale: Produces a whose clause, which replaces the possessive.

prompt: Rewrite in the passive, starting with 'The bridge': 'Workers built the bridge in 1920.'

key_points.text: Uses was built
Keeps the date

model_answers: The bridge was built in 1920.
The bridge was built by workers in 1920.

guards.note: the passive needs was built

anchors.text: The bridge was built in 1920.
The bridge built in 1920.
The bridge was build in 1920.

rationale: Forms a past simple passive with an irregular participle.

prompt: Rewrite in the passive, starting with 'The results': 'The school will announce the results on Monday.'

key_points.text: Uses will be announced
Keeps 'on Monday'

model_answers: The results will be announced on Monday.
The results will be announced by the school on Monday.

guards.note: the passive needs will be announced

anchors.text: The results will be announced on Monday.
The results will announced on Monday.
The results are announced on Monday.

rationale: Forms a future passive.

prompt: Your friend has a toothache. Give advice in one sentence using should.

key_points.text: Uses should with a bare verb (no to)
The advice suits a toothache

model_answers: You should see a dentist today.

guards.note: should takes a verb without to

anchors.text: You should see a dentist today.
You should to see a dentist.
You should eat more sweets.

rationale: Produces should for advice, with the bare infinitive.

prompt: Explain the difference in one or two sentences: 'You mustn't bring your phone' and 'You don't have to bring your phone'.

key_points.text: mustn't means it is not allowed
don't have to means it is not necessary (you may choose)

model_answers: Mustn't means you are not allowed to bring it; don't have to means it is not necessary, but you can if you want.

anchors.text: Mustn't means you are not allowed to bring it; don't have to means it isn't necessary.
They both mean you cannot bring your phone.
Mustn't means it's forbidden. Don't have to means you can choose.

rationale: Explains a meaning contrast in words; only an evaluator can judge it.

prompt: Rewrite the sentence, replacing 'nice' and 'went' with more precise words: 'We had a nice day and went home.'

key_points.text: Replaces nice with a more precise adjective
Replaces went with a more precise verb

model_answers: We had a relaxing day and strolled home.
We had a sunny day and hurried home.

guards.note: nice must be replaced
went must be replaced

anchors.text: We had a wonderful day and wandered home.
We had a good day and went home.
We had an exciting day and went home.

rationale: Produces precise replacements; code can only check that the general words are gone.

prompt: Make this sentence from a science report precise: 'The water got really hot after a while.'

key_points.text: Gives a measured temperature
Gives a measured time
Leaves out informal words (got, really)

model_answers: The water reached 80 °C after 5 minutes.

guards.note: a temperature needs a number
a time needs a number and a unit

anchors.text: The temperature of the water rose to 95 °C after 8 minutes.
The water got very hot after some time.
The water became hot after 4 minutes.

rationale: Precise wording for a report; code checks only that numbers are present.

prompt: Use the word 'result' in one sentence about a science experiment.

key_points.text: Uses result to mean what happened at the end of the experiment
Writes a complete sentence

model_answers: The result of our experiment showed that plants need light.

guards.note: the word result must be used

anchors.text: The result of our experiment showed that plants need light.
I result the experiment.
The result was that the ice melted faster in the sun.

rationale: Uses an academic word in its subject sense, in the learner's own sentence.

prompt: 'The classroom was an oven.' Explain in one sentence what this metaphor means.

key_points.text: Says the classroom was very hot
Shows it is a comparison, not a real oven

model_answers: It means the classroom was extremely hot, like the inside of an oven.

anchors.text: It means the classroom was extremely hot, like the inside of an oven.
The classroom had an oven in it for cooking.
It was really hot in the classroom.

rationale: Explains a simple metaphor in words.

prompt: 'Her words were a warm blanket.' What does this suggest about how the listener felt? Answer in one or two sentences.

key_points.text: The listener felt comforted, safe or calmer
Links this to what a warm blanket does

model_answers: The listener felt comforted and safe, because her kind words made them feel the way a warm blanket does.

anchors.text: The listener felt comforted and safe, as if wrapped in something warm.
She gave the listener a blanket because it was cold.
They felt better and less worried.

rationale: Interprets the feeling a less familiar metaphor creates.

prompt: Join the two sentences with although: 'It was raining. We played outside.'

key_points.text: Uses although to join the contrast
Keeps both ideas, with no extra but

model_answers: Although it was raining, we played outside.
We played outside although it was raining.

guards.note: although must be used
although and but together double the link

anchors.text: Although it was raining, we played outside.
Although it was raining, but we played outside.
It was raining, so we played outside.

rationale: Joins a contrast with although, produced.

prompt: Finish the sentence with a precaution: 'Take a torch in case ...'

key_points.text: Gives something that might happen
Uses a present-tense clause after in case (not will)

model_answers: Take a torch in case the power goes off.
Take a torch in case it gets dark before we come back.

guards.note: in case takes the present, not will

anchors.text: Take a torch in case the power goes off.
Take a torch in case the lights will go out.
Take a torch in case so you can see.

rationale: Completes a precaution clause.

prompt: Fix this run-on sentence: 'The bus was late, we missed the start of the film.'

key_points.text: Separates or properly joins the two clauses (full stop, semicolon or a joining word)
Keeps both ideas

model_answers: The bus was late, so we missed the start of the film.
The bus was late. We missed the start of the film.
Because the bus was late, we missed the start of the film.

guards.note: the comma splice is still there

anchors.text: The bus was late, so we missed the start of the film.
The bus was late, we missed the start of the film.
The bus was late; we missed the start of the film.

rationale: Repairs a comma splice in the learner's own words.

prompt: Join with the best joining word: 'I was hungry. There was no food in the house.'

key_points.text: Uses but (or yet) to show the contrast

model_answers: I was hungry, but there was no food in the house.

guards.note: a contrast needs but or yet

anchors.text: I was hungry, but there was no food in the house.
I was hungry, so there was no food in the house.
I was hungry but there was no food.

rationale: Chooses and writes a contrast coordinator.

prompt: Combine into one sentence starting with 'Hearing the bell': 'Arun heard the bell. Arun ran to the gate.'

key_points.text: Starts with Hearing the bell
The subject straight after the phrase is Arun (or he), so it does not dangle

model_answers: Hearing the bell, Arun ran to the gate.

guards.note: must start with Hearing the bell
the subject after the phrase must be Arun or he

anchors.text: Hearing the bell, Arun ran to the gate.
Hearing the bell, the gate was where Arun ran.
Hearing the bell, Arun's bag fell off.

rationale: Produces a participle opening that attaches to the right subject.

prompt: Write a second sentence beginning with 'As a result' that follows from: 'Heavy rain flooded the main road.'

key_points.text: Begins with As a result
Gives a sensible consequence of the flooding

model_answers: As a result, the school buses could not run.

guards.note: must begin with As a result

anchors.text: As a result, the school buses could not run.
As a result, it rained heavily.
However, the buses could not run.

rationale: Writes a result sentence that fits the connective.

prompt: Fix this so it is one complete sentence: 'We stayed inside. Because it was raining.'

key_points.text: Joins the because-clause to the main clause

model_answers: We stayed inside because it was raining.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.

guards.note: the because-clause is still on its own

anchors.text: We stayed inside because it was raining.
We stayed inside. Because it was raining.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.

rationale: Repairs a subordinate-clause fragment.

prompt: Rewrite this message for your head teacher: 'Hey! Can u let our class go on a trip pls?'

key_points.text: Makes a polite, formal request (for example, Could you … or I would like to ask …)
Removes text-speak and slang (Hey, u, pls)

model_answers: Could you please allow our class to go on a trip?
I would like to ask whether our class may go on a trip.

guards.note: text-speak or slang remains

anchors.text: Could you please allow our class to go on a trip?
Hey, could u let our class go on a trip please?
Our class wants a trip.

rationale: Changes register for an adult reader, in the learner's own words.

prompt: Rewrite this sentence from a formal letter of complaint so that it keeps a formal register: 'Your shop sold me a rubbish phone and I'm well annoyed.'

key_points.text: States the problem formally (for example, a faulty phone)
Expresses displeasure formally (for example, I am disappointed)
No slang (rubbish, well annoyed)

model_answers: I am writing to complain that the phone I bought from your shop is faulty, and I am very disappointed.

guards.note: slang remains

anchors.text: The phone I purchased from your store is defective, and I am dissatisfied with the service.
Your shop sold me a faulty phone and I'm well annoyed.
I am writing to complain that the phone I bought is faulty, and I am disappointed.

rationale: Keeps a formal register throughout one sentence.

prompt: Add one sentence that gives a reason or an example for this idea: 'Our school should have a garden.'

key_points.text: Gives a relevant reason or example

model_answers: Students could grow vegetables and learn how plants grow.

anchors.text: Students could grow vegetables and learn how plants grow.
My uncle has a red car.
It would give us a cool, green place to read at lunchtime.

rationale: Develops an idea with one relevant reason; relevance can only be judged by reading.

prompt: Develop this point in two sentences, explaining why it matters: 'Libraries are important.'

key_points.text: Gives a specific reason, not a repeat of the point
Explains the effect or importance of that reason

model_answers: Libraries give free books to families who cannot buy them. This means every child can read widely, whatever their family can afford.

anchors.text: Libraries give free books to families who cannot buy them. This means every child can read widely.
Libraries are very important. Everyone needs libraries.
Libraries let students borrow books for free.

rationale: Develops a point with a reason and its consequence.

prompt: Write one or two sentences persuading your principal to allow a longer lunch break. Give a reason.

key_points.text: States the position (a longer lunch break)
Gives a relevant reason

model_answers: Please allow a longer lunch break, because students need time to eat properly and rest before afternoon lessons.

anchors.text: Please allow a longer lunch break, because students need time to eat properly and rest.
I like lunch.
We should have a longer lunch break.

rationale: States a position with a supporting reason.

prompt: Write one or two sentences that answer this counter-argument: 'A longer school day would make students too tired.'

key_points.text: Acknowledges the concern
Gives a reason or evidence that answers it

model_answers: It is true that a longer day could be tiring; however, if the extra time is used for sport and clubs, students may go home more refreshed.

anchors.text: It is true that a longer day could be tiring; however, if the extra hour is for sport, students may feel more refreshed.
That is wrong because it is wrong.
Students would not be tired, because the extra hour would be for games, not lessons.

rationale: Concedes and rebuts in one or two sentences.

prompt: Write only the greeting and the closing of a short email to your cousin Anu, on two lines.

key_points.text: An informal greeting addressed to Anu
An informal closing

model_answers:
Hi Anu,
Love, Ravi

guards.note: the greeting must name Anu

anchors.text:
Hi Anu,
See you soon, Ravi

Dear Sir or Madam,
Yours faithfully, Ravi

Hi Anu,
Yours faithfully, Ravi Kumar

rationale: Produces informal email conventions.

prompt: Write a subject line for a formal letter to the Municipal Commissioner about broken street lights in your colony.

key_points.text: Names the problem (broken street lights)
States the purpose formally (for example, Request to repair …, Complaint regarding …)

model_answers: Subject: Request to repair broken street lights in Lake View Colony

guards.note: the problem must be named

anchors.text: Subject: Request to repair broken street lights in Lake View Colony
Lights!!!
Subject: Complaint regarding non-functional street lights

rationale: Writes a precise, formal subject line.

prompt: Why did Meena lose her kite? Answer in one sentence.

key_points.text: The string snapped (broke)

model_answers: She lost it because the string snapped in the strong wind.

guards.note: the answer must say the string broke

anchors.text: She lost it because the string snapped in the strong wind.
Her brother took it.
The string broke and the kite flew away.

rationale: States a cause given in a different sentence, in the learner's words.

prompt: Why did everyone say that Lakshmi the goat had been cleverer than all of them? Answer in one or two sentences.

key_points.text: She refused to stay in her shed
The shed was blown away, so she was safe

model_answers: Because she refused to stay in her shed, and in the morning the shed had been blown away, so she was safe.

anchors.text: Because she refused to stay in her shed, and in the morning the shed had blown away.
Because she could open doors.
The shed was carried away by the wind.

rationale: Links two facts into an inferred cause.

prompt: Why did Kiran take a deep breath instead of shouting at Dev? Answer in one or two sentences.

key_points.text: She saw that Dev was sorry or upset
She chose to stay calm so as not to upset him more

model_answers: She saw how sorry Dev was, so she decided to stay calm instead of making him feel worse.

anchors.text: She saw how sorry Dev was, so she decided to stay calm.
She was tired from making the volcano.
Because Dev was crying and said sorry.

prompt: Why does Mr. Iyer put down his pen and look at Kavya for the first time? Answer in one or two sentences.

key_points.text: Her honest, unexpected answer surprised or interested him
It was not the safe, rehearsed answer he expected

model_answers: Her honest answer about wanting the magazine to be braver surprised him, because it was not the safe, rehearsed answer he expected.

anchors.text: Her honest answer surprised him, because it was not the safe answer he expected.
Because he had finished writing.
He was interested in what she said about the magazine.

prompt: Summarise 'Why Do Cities Get Hotter?' in one or two sentences.

key_points.text: Cities are hotter than the countryside
Gives the main causes (dark surfaces, fewer plants, heat from machines)
Says cities are trying to cool down

model_answers: Cities are hotter than the countryside because of dark surfaces, fewer plants and heat from machines, and some cities are now trying to cool down.

anchors.text: Cities are hotter than the countryside because of dark roads, fewer plants and machines, and some are trying to cool down.
Singapore has gardens on its roofs.
Cities are hotter because roads are dark and there are fewer trees.
